Sinuous

/SIN-yoo-us/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sinuous means winding and curving in a graceful, snake-like way.

From the canyon rim the river below looked like a sinuous ribbon of silver, folding back on itself again and again.

Worked Example

The old post road between the two valley towns covers nine kilometres as the crow flies, yet drivers travel twenty-six kilometres getting from one to the other. The road never runs straight for more than a hundred metres: it swings left around a rock spur, curves right along a stream, and doubles back on itself twice near the summit. Tour buses are banned because they cannot follow the bends. Cyclists love the road for exactly that reason, since its sinuous course makes every kilometre a new turn.

Twenty-six kilometres of continuous bends to cover nine kilometres of straight-line distance, with no stretch straight for more than a hundred metres, is precisely the smooth, snake-like winding that sinuous describes.

How Sinuous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

winding

winding: bending repeatedly along its length

serpentine

serpentine: curving like a moving snake

Antonyms

straight

straight: running without any bend at all

direct

direct: going from one point to another by the shortest line

How Strong Is It? — curved → sinuous → serpentine

curved vs. sinuous

curved vs. sinuous: Curved describes a single bend, while sinuous means the bending repeats, one graceful turn after another.

serpentine vs. sinuous

serpentine vs. sinuous: Serpentine is the most vivid word in the group: it insists on the image of a snake in motion, while sinuous can describe any smoothly winding shape.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of sinuous.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sinu-

Root — sinu-: a bend, curve, or fold (Latin sinus)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of; characterized by

Put it together

Put it together: Latin sinus named a curve or a fold: the fold of a toga, the bend of a bay, and the hollow curves in the skull that doctors still call the sinuses. Add -ous, meaning 'full of,' and sinuous is literally 'full of curves.' The same root winds through insinuate, which originally described working one's way in along an indirect, curving path.

Use the root in a new word: insinuate

Use the root in a new word: insinuate: To insinuate yourself into a group is literally to wind your way in by curves rather than walk in straight, from the same Latin sinus (a bend or curve) that gives us sinuous.

Root Check

Word Choice

descriptive; usually admiring

Sinuous is a compliment more often than not, since it suggests grace in the curving, which is why it suits rivers, dancers, and coastlines but sounds odd applied to something merely crooked or damaged. Keep it for smooth, continuous curves: a path that turns in sharp right angles is angular or zigzagging, not sinuous.
